import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "RANK(TS_MEAN($vwap * $volume, 20) / (TS_MEAN($vwap * $volume, 120) + 1e-8))" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "TURNOVER_SURGE_20_120" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)
7cffba054d4502c8.factor_description: Implements the Miller (1977) / Scheinkman-Xiong (2003) resale-option premium proxy for the A-share no-short-sale regime. Daily yuan turnover is defined as $vwap x $volume. The factor is the ratio of the 20-day trailing mean to the 120-day trailing mean of turnover, so each stock's short-run turnover surge is scaled by its own long-run baseline; this removes persistent firm size and liquidity differences that would otherwise dominate a raw cross-sectional turnover rank. Because pessimists can only abstain when short selling is unavailable, abnormally high churn marks names whose marginal buyers are optimists and whose prices carry a resale-option premium; as retail attention mean-reverts within weeks, this premium deflates, so HIGH factor values predict LOWER forward returns over the next 10-20 trading days (committed negative RankIC, strongest in retail-driven bull phases). The 120-day rolling mean is undefined (null) until the long history is complete, which automatically nulls the factor for newly listed or insufficient-history stocks.

For each instrument on day t, the 5-day cumulative return R5 is computed as the compounded product of (1 + daily return) over the last 5 daily bars minus 1, then percentile-ranked within the cross-section on that date into [0,1], so a higher rank means a larger past 5-day gain. db4078aae5a8478b.factor_description: Lottery extreme-gain score net of limit-up truncation artifacts. Each day, for every instrument, the tail-gain score is the average of the rolling 75th and 95th percentiles of daily returns over the past 20 trading days: with 20 observations the 0.75 quantile is the 5th-largest daily return and the 0.95 quantile the largest, so their average proxies the mean of the 5 largest daily gains (the hypothesis's lottery salience marker). The score is ranked cross-sectionally, then orthogonalized against the same-window (20-day) count of daily returns above 9.5% (the limit-up-day count in the A-share price-limit regime, covering both the ~10% and ~20% limit-up bands) by subtracting the cross-sectional correlation times the z-scored count. The residual has zero same-day cross-sectional correlation with the limit-up count, isolating genuine lottery demand from truncation-driven tail gains. High residual = recently extreme-gain lottery name whose tail gains are not mere limit-up artifacts; under retail lottery demand with no short sellers such names are overpriced, so the factor is expected to carry NEGATIVE rank IC against 10-20 day forward returns, strongest in high-turnover speculative episodes. Hyperparameters: tail window = 20 days, quantiles = 0.75 and 0.95, limit-up threshold = 9.5%, count window = 20 days.
db4078aae5a8478b.factor_formulation: F_t = z^Y_t - \rho_t z^X_t, \quad Y_t = \mathrm{Rank}\left(\frac{Q^{(20)}_{0.75}(r)_t + Q^{(20)}_{0.95}(r)_t}{2}\right), \quad X_t = \sum_{i=0}^{19} \mathbf{1}\{r_{t-i} > 0.095\}, \quad \rho_t = \overline{z^Y_t z^X_t}

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.function_lib import *


def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe
    df = pd.read_hdf('./daily_pv.h5', key='data')
    
    expr = parse_symbol(expr, df.columns)
    expr = parse_expression(expr)

    # replace '$var' by 'df['var'] to extract var's actual values
    for col in df.columns:
        expr = expr.replace(col[1:], f"df[\'{col}\']")

    df[name] = eval(expr)
    result = df[name].astype(np.float64)

    if os.path.exists('result.h5'):
        os.remove('result.h5')
    result.to_hdf('result.h5', key='data')

if __name__ == '__main__':
    # Input factor expression. Do NOT use the variable format like "df['$xxx']" in factor expressions. Instead, you should use "$xxx". 
    expr = "ZSCORE(TS_QUANTILE($return, 20, 0.75) / (DELAY(TS_MEAN(ABS($return), 60), 20) + 1e-8))" # Your output factor expression will be filled in here
    name = "EXTREME_GAIN_RATIO_20D" # Your output factor name will be filled in here
    calculate_factor(expr, name)
8b9f896e56cb1ff9.factor_description: Scale-free lottery-demand marker for a retail-dominated, no-shorting, limit-board market: daily gains that are extreme relative to the stock's own typical move mark overpricing that unwinds over the next 1-20 days. Numerator: the 75th percentile of daily returns over the past 20 sessions (q = 1 - 5/20 = 0.75), i.e. approximately the 5th-largest daily return, a robust lower-bound proxy for the mean of the 5 largest returns that is exact when extreme gains cluster at the limit-up cap (limit-up streaks). Denominator: the mean absolute daily return over the 60 sessions ending 20 days back (the pre-event typical move), delayed so the event window cannot contaminate its own baseline. The ratio expresses the recent jump in multiples of the stock's own typical daily move, de-conflating limit-up truncation: a limit-up streak in a formerly sleepy name scores far higher than the same streak in a chronically volatile name. Because skewness-preferring retail overweights such lottery jumps and no short sellers compete the overpricing away, HIGH values predict LOWER forward returns (negative IC), most strongly in high-turnover names and speculative episodes. Hyperparameters: event window 20 days, top-k 5 (quantile 0.75), baseline window 60 days delayed 20 days, epsilon 1e-8, daily cross-sectional z-score, evaluation horizons 1/5/20 days.

import os
from quantaalpha.factors.coder.expr_parser import parse_expression, parse_symbol

def calculate_factor(expr: str, name: str):
    # stock dataframe

if __name__ == '__main__':
